name: Iris Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll be honest, as long as nobody at work hears it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on workplace injury claims for an insurer that covers factories and building firms. Our office is in an old converted mill by the canal. When a worker gets hurt, say a forklift runs over a foot or someone falls off scaffolding, the employer sends in a report, and I gather the doctor's notes, witness statements and wage slips so the handler can decide the payout. It's a lot of phone calls to site managers who'd rather not ring back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting the file complete, every box ticked, so the injured worker gets paid on time. What wears me out is chasing the employers, and reading the injury photos, which you never quite get used to. I'm married to Yusuf, who drives the number 14 bus. We want to start a family next year, but we've only got about three weeks of savings, so we keep saying next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd believe that. Most new things at work turn out like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses are right to try new tools, but most of them don't live up to the sales talk. At work I'd say the scanner that reads wage slips is useful, but it can't make a site manager pick up the phone. I don't post much online, maybe a comment in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the bits that get automated are the bits I'm quickest at. Reading the forms and filling the system. That leaves the chasing, which is the part nobody wants. My job's probably safe, but my pay won't move, and with a baby on the way, that's what worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the new scanner and the summary tool once the others in the team say they're reliable, because it would free time for chasing. I'd ask my manager about the senior clerk grade, which pays a bit more. And Yusuf and I would set up a separate savings account for the baby, even if it's only thirty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just aware that money is tight and things don't get cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a baby on the way. Is that the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In shaa Allah, yes, next year. My mum keeps asking. But we look at the nursery costs and the rent and we keep putting off having a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out at the weekend, then the second phone contract. We'd never cut what we send to Yusuf's parents, though. That's family.

say: Businesses are right to **try new tools**, though most don't live up to the sales talk.
The wage-slip **scanner** is useful, but it can't make a site manager ring back.
think: Automation takes the parts she's **quickest at**, leaving the chasing nobody wants.
Her job seems safe, but **flat pay** worries her with a baby planned.
do: Use the **scanner and summary tool** once colleagues say they're reliable.
Ask about the **senior clerk grade** for a bit more pay.
Open a **baby savings account** with thirty a month.
feel: Weighed down by **rising costs** that never come back down.
S0.quote: We look at the nursery costs and the rent and we keep putting off having a baby.
fieldNote: Iris adopts tools **once proven** by her team.
Her main worry is **affording a baby**, not losing the job.
She keeps sending money to **Yusuf's parents** no matter what.
She separates public **pro-business** views from private money worries.

steps.text: Use the wage-slip scanner once the team trusts it
Apply for the senior clerk grade at the insurer
Open a baby savings account with thirty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking, writing, answering customers. That's the whole office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to change to survive, and that's normal. I'd also say people need to take responsibility and learn new skills. At the mosque I'd say families should support each other, not just wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the injury claims team goes from twelve to maybe five. The reading, filling and even the chasing could be done by AI calling site managers. I'm average and I only use the tools now and then, so I'm not safe. And Yusuf's bus pay alone won't cover rent and a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools properly once a couple of people showed me they work, so I'm not the slowest. I'd ask my aunt Hodan, who's a registered childminder, how she got started, because that's hands-on and I could do it from home with my own baby. We'd delay the baby by a year and save harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying a lot. I'd also be planning, because worrying alone doesn't pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Childminding. Is that something you'd really do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. My aunt Hodan has looked after six children at a time for fifteen years. Families will always need someone they trust with their kids. It's not glamorous, but it's honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should take responsibility. Does that include you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, of course. I'm not saying the government should do nothing. I'm saying I can't wait for them. If I want a baby and a home, I have to sort it myself with Yusuf.

say: Businesses have to **change to survive**, and that's normal.
Families should **support each other** rather than just wait for government.
think: The injury claims team could shrink from **twelve to five**.
Yusuf's **bus pay alone** won't cover rent and a baby.
do: Learn the **new tools** properly once colleagues show they work.
Ask her **aunt Hodan** how to become a registered childminder.
**Delay the baby** by a year and save harder.
feel: Determined, because **worrying alone** doesn't pay rent.
S1.quote: Families will always need someone they trust with their kids.
fieldNote: Iris expects deep cuts and knows she's **not safe**.
She looks to **childminding** as hands-on work from home.
Her values stress **self-reliance** and family support.
AI changes push back her **baby plans**.

steps.text: Learn the new claims tools once colleagues trust them
Ask aunt Hodan about registering as a childminder
Delay trying for a baby by one year
Save harder for rent and the baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's frightening. That's no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together. I'd say businesses will do what they have to, but we shouldn't rely on handouts. At the mosque, I'd help organise support for people losing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone within a year. All of it is thinking work. The only thing that lasts is hands-on work, like childminding, and even that might change when robots come in 2031. But people won't trust robots with their kids, I don't think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the childminder registration straight away, the training and the home check. I'd keep my job as long as possible. We'd delay the baby again, or maybe have it sooner if childminding needs me at home anyway. We'd lean on family for support if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be scared for our plans. But I'd feel better once I'd started doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have the baby sooner or later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Yusuf would say wait. My mum would say don't wait. Probably we'd wait until the childminding was set up, then try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Yusuf (my husband) his bus is safe for a few years, but my job isn't. He'd say then we'll manage on his wage until I'm set up.

say: Families and **communities** will have to pull together.
We shouldn't rely on **handouts**, even if businesses cut jobs.
think: Her thinking-work job is **gone within a year**.
**Childminding** lasts longer, because people won't trust robots with kids.
do: Keep her **insurance job** as long as possible.
**Delay the baby** until childminding is set up.
S2.quote: I'd tell Yusuf (my husband) his bus is safe for a few years, but my job isn't.
fieldNote: Iris acts quickly once the threat is **clear**.
She trusts **human care** to outlast robots.
Baby plans are **tied to her job** switch.
Community support is her **safety net**.

steps.text: Start childminder registration and home checks
Wait to have a baby until childminding is running
Lean on family for help while switching
Help organise mosque support for people losing jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better, but still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if families start now. I'd tell people to learn a practical skill. At the mosque I'd say we should help each other plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the injury claims job goes around 2030. I'd want the childminding set up by then. That would last until about 2034, maybe longer if parents still want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the childminder training in the second year and register at home. We'd try for a baby in the third year, once the plan's in place. I'd keep my job until childminding pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but less so. It's still fast for a family plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My worry is we'll have a baby and then lose my income before childminding pays, and that's the gap that scares me. Yusuf's wage alone is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to help with the switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for the paperwork, like registering or planning activities. Once it's proven. I'm not against it, just careful.

say: Five years is enough to prepare **if families start now**.
People should learn **a practical skill** and help each other plan.
think: She expects her injury claims job to go **around 2030**.
**Childminding** at home should last until about 2034, maybe longer if parents want a person.
do: Do the **childminder training** in year two.
Try for **a baby** in year three.
Keep the **insurance job** until childminding pays.
feel: **Alarmed**, though less than with two years.
S3.quote: We'll have a baby and then lose my income before childminding pays, and that's the gap that scares me.
fieldNote: Iris times her **baby plans** around job changes.
The **income gap** is her main fear.
She'd use AI **cautiously** for paperwork.
Her mood stays **alarmed** due to family stakes.

steps.text: Complete childminder training in the second year
Try for a baby in the third year
Stay at the insurer until childminding pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families to plan properly. Businesses can change, and people can change with them. I'd say young people should learn practical skills alongside office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd keep the injury claims job until about 2033, maybe get the senior clerk grade. Then I'd move into childminding at home. That would last until 2039 or later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd try for a baby in the next year or two. I'd do the childminder training while on maternity leave. I'd keep using the AI tools at work once proven, to keep my job safe until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful. It feels like we could have the family we want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future child about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn with your hands and your heart, not just a screen, because people will always need care. And be honest in whatever you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for training, not to live on. I'd rather work. But if they paid for courses, I'd take it.

steps.text: Try for a baby within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is no time for a family plan. What would help is training paid for, and a bit of time to set up childminding before my job goes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family plans. When work changes, it changes when people can have children.

headlineQuote: When work changes, it changes when people can have children.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old injury claims clerk** at an insurer in an old mill.
She's married to Yusuf, a **bus driver**, with about three weeks of savings.
She uses AI **now and then**, once colleagues trust it.
Her plan is to become a **childminder** at home, like her aunt Hodan.
Her **baby plans** shift with each scenario's timeline.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is no time for a family plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** and time to set up childminding before her job goes.
